blocks.text: In my late twenties I joined what I thought was a mid-sized company. It turned out I was employee number one at a legal entity being spun off. I had sold myself as someone who could do the work of ten, and that was exactly the seat I was hired into. For the six months it took to finish the spin-off, I had no benefits and did every odd job there was.

But I was fine with it, because the work was fascinating. As the founder's right hand I was trusted with everything, and I got to do the work of ten. We were so deep in it that we lost track of time, and in barely three years the company had grown past fifty people and three million dollars in exports.

I built every team — production, order management, customer support, shipping, planning — and organizing their work taught me as much through failure as success. Gathering opinions was hard, and more than once I made busy people's work more complicated in the name of structure. But I was good at reading how work actually happened, and removing unnecessary work while building process kept paying off.

Later, as head of new business, I got us to where we could run two or three ventures at once. That meant learning management, finance and accounting too, and it gave me a working understanding of an entire organization. Through all of it, one question never left me.
“How do we talk as little as possible and still do exactly the work that matters?”

Working more and more closely with engineering teams, I started using issue trackers built around projects. Listing the work, sorting by priority and importance, even estimating how long each piece would take — I thought I had found the answer.
“Plan the week, then focus on what truly has to happen today.”

Shipping ran on today's shipping list. Orders, production and customer teams organized everything except genuine emergencies into planned work and work due today, so that all anyone had to look at was [today's to-do]. That alone produced real results.

I also went after unnecessary work directly. Moving a file into a server folder advanced the task stage and assigned the right person automatically, so whoever managed files never had to click anything. Scanning a barcode on an outgoing item moved its stage, stamped the date, and closed out every task attached to it.

Before founding my own company I worked as a PM at a development agency, building systems and ERPs, and I folded all of that into how I plan products. After founding it, I built for fully remote work by making a system that doesn't need to be administered — people plan their own work and manage their own time.
One hour of meetings per week was the motto.

I never doubted the people; I worried whether revenue would keep growing without me in the middle of it. That worry was gone within six months of going fully remote. Given complete ownership of their hours and their work, people simply got it done — wherever they were, whenever they worked.

In the end, outstanding results assume good people, and become possible when the system underneath them is sound. I studied entrepreneurship for my master's and I'm writing on the same subject in my DBA — the question of how work gets managed has never let go of me.

story.closing: My work to keep work from becoming a burden isn't finished, and PlanQ sits on that road. PlanQ is a work management platform that connects tasks and projects, people and time, clients and billing. The way I kept searching for on the floor — we are building it into a tool.

why.title: Why design the work system first?
why.p0: When something breaks, most companies buy another program. But most problems start in the operating system, not in the software.
why.p1: If the work itself is unclear, AI adds nothing, automation stalls halfway, and even a great tool ends up unused.
why.p2: A tool will not decide how you work for you.
why.p3: So we design before we build. First we make explicit how the company actually works — then we put the system on top of it.

low.now: The core work and roles mean different things to different people.
low.change: Map how revenue is made on one page and name an owner for each step.
low.planq: In PlanQ: build that flow as projects and task groups, with owners attached.

mid.now: The big picture is shared but not written down.
mid.change: Pick one bottleneck and define just that stretch: steps, owner, deadline.
mid.planq: In PlanQ: save the repeating structure as a task template and reuse it.

high.now: Your work structure is clear and shared.
high.change: Check whether a new hire could follow it in a day.
high.planq: In PlanQ: project templates keep that structure identical across the team.

low.now: Requests arrive everywhere, so it's unclear who owns them.
low.change: Collect requests in one place and set an owner and due date on arrival. Keep approvals as defined steps.
low.planq: In PlanQ: requests from Q talk and Q mail become Q tasks, and request → review → done is recorded.

mid.now: Owners are set, but approvals are scattered.
mid.change: For work that needs sign-off, move review → approval into one place.
mid.planq: In PlanQ: add a reviewer and every review, revision and approval stays on the task.

high.now: Request-to-done runs on a defined flow.
high.change: Measure which step most often causes delays.
high.planq: In PlanQ: weekly reports and overdue flags show that step at a glance.

low.now: Files and customer history live in people’s heads.
low.change: Start by gathering conversations, files and tasks per customer in one place.
low.planq: In PlanQ: one customer page brings together chat, mail, tasks and billing.

mid.now: It can be found, but only by searching several places.
mid.change: Pick the five things you look up most and pin them in one place.
mid.planq: In PlanQ: Q file and Q info attach materials to projects and customers.

high.now: Information is in one place and anyone can pick it up.
high.change: Review the line between what customers see and what stays internal.
high.planq: In PlanQ: visibility levels set that line on every item.

low.now: Almost every decision lands on the owner.
low.change: Pick one area — budget, scope or schedule — and write down what the team can decide alone.
low.planq: In PlanQ: per-member permissions and review policies put that rule in the system.

mid.now: There are implicit rules, but decisions are scattered.
mid.change: Make a habit of logging each decision in one line on the related task or doc.
mid.planq: In PlanQ: decisions stay in task comments, history and project notes.

high.now: Decision rules and records are in place.
high.change: See which recurring decisions could become rules.
high.planq: In PlanQ: recurring tasks and templates run those rules for you.

low.now: Repeat work is done by hand every time.
low.change: List three weekly tasks and standardise just one first.
low.planq: In PlanQ: recurring tasks and scheduled invoices recreate that work automatically.

mid.now: There are templates, but still lots of manual work.
mid.change: Instead of everyone using AI separately, attach it to one step of the team flow.
mid.planq: In PlanQ: Cue extracts tasks from chats and summarises meetings straight into tasks.

high.now: Much of your repeat work is automated.
high.change: Check who notices when an automation fails.
high.planq: In PlanQ: the Needs-attention list surfaces only what a person must check.

low.now: There are many tools and they don’t connect.
low.change: Start by bringing customer communication and task management into one tool.
low.planq: In PlanQ: chat, tasks, files and billing connect on one screen.

mid.now: You use a few tools, partly connected.
mid.change: Give customers one link where they can follow progress themselves.
mid.planq: In PlanQ: one client link shows progress, files and invoices.

high.now: Tools are consolidated and customers see everything in one place.
high.change: Next, let AI read that data and act on it.
high.planq: In PlanQ: connect ChatGPT or Claude to look up and create work in plain language.

detailsPage.title: Details that surprise you
detailsPage.sub: Small everyday moments save more time than big features. All of these are already in PlanQ.
detailsPage.closingTitle: Details are best felt by using them
detailsPage.closingSub: Try every feature free for 14 days.
detailsPage.homeSub: We took care of the small everyday moments.

chatgpt.title: Tell ChatGPT, and the task appears in PlanQ
chatgpt.body: Ask «my tasks this week» or «save this call as a consultation» in chat. Due-date changes and completion ask once more; deleting, sending and billing are never possible.

replyDraft.title: A reply draft in one click, in the sender's language
replyDraft.body: It draws on the recent thread and your FAQ. Refine it with requests like «shorter» — your own edits are never overwritten.

noteAnswer.title: When a question comes up in a meeting, the answer is already being prepared
noteAnswer.body: Alongside live transcription and translation, it picks evidence from your Q&A and documents to prepare an answer.

estimate.title: AI time estimates follow your team's own history
estimate.body: The same task title gets a different estimate in each team.

guestLink.title: Clients join with a single link — no sign-up
guestLink.body: Chat, signing, invoice payment and booking all work from a link. No need to ask clients to install anything.

booking.title: Clients pick a consultation slot themselves
booking.body: Only your open hours show. Once confirmed, a calendar file and a video-call link are sent.
booking.cond: Client desk setup · Video calls need the owner's Google account

realInquiry.title: Promotional mail stays out of your consultations
realInquiry.body: Real inquiries are picked by «did we reply? is it a personal address?», not keywords. Anything missed is one right-click away.

oneClient.title: Mail, chat and meeting notes gather on one client
oneClient.body: The consultation history builds up in one place instead of scattering.

chatTranslate.title: Chat is translated into two languages as you send
chatTranslate.body: Talk with overseas clients, each in their own language.

popout.title: Your task list floats above Excel while you work
popout.body: Keep it on top of other apps and start or stop tasks right there.

approveDone.title: Approval doesn't close the task until the owner confirms
approveDone.body: The owner sees the approval and wraps up — nothing slips through.

responsibility.title: Only the requester edits the brief; only the owner edits the result
responsibility.body: No one overwrites by rank, so every change has an owner.

autoHours.title: Time worked adds itself up
autoHours.body: Time spent «in progress» is collected into actual hours.

duplicate.title: Copies bring the content, not the signatures or share links
duplicate.body: A copy never passes for the original.

toc.title: Document outlines build themselves and never go stale
toc.body: Edit a heading and the outline updates instantly.

pinTab.title: Pin your go-to documents as project tabs
pinTab.body: Open the project and the document is right there.

autosave.title: There is no save button
autosave.body: Everything saves as you type — even the last keystroke when you leave the screen.

drafts.title: Half-written comments don't disappear
drafts.body: Close the task and come back — your words are still there.

history.title: Roll back from the history any time
history.body: Edit freely, even without a save button.

liveShare.title: Edit while a share link is open, and the viewer sees it too
liveShare.body: Clients never keep reading an outdated version.

privateNote.title: Meeting notes are truly yours
privateNote.body: Only the scope you open is visible — not even the owner can look.

infoTable.title: Define your own fields in the info library
infoTable.body: Ten field types including number, date, choice and checkbox. Secret fields stay masked and out of search and AI.

driveImport.title: Bring in Google Drive files straight from the attach window
driveImport.body: Once imported they become PlanQ files anyone on the team can open.

trash.title: One trash for everything
trash.body: Restore files, documents and info from one place.

dedup.title: The same file is stored only once
dedup.body: Upload it again and again — storage is used once.

export.title: Take your files with you as a zip
export.body: Download your files, documents and meeting notes in one go.

signField.title: Place a signature field and the signature lands right there
signField.body: The text is frozen when you request, and the signed PDF comes with a certificate.

invoiceLink.title: One invoice link for payment notice, card payment and tax invoices
invoiceLink.body: Everything the client needs to do is on a single link.
invoiceLink.cond: Card payment needs your Stripe account

installments.title: Bill in installments — deposit, interim, balance
installments.body: Track payment and receipts per installment.

autoAttend.title: Starting a task clocks you in
autoAttend.body: Colleagues see only «working»; times are visible to you and admins.

profitHour.title: See profit per hour by project and client
profitHour.body: Actual hours and rates show where you gain and where you leak.

badgeSum.title: The to-check count equals the menu badges
badgeSum.body: Nothing is counted twice, so you can trust the numbers.
